A1.justification: These are versions of the same benchmark, renamed from StructBench to StrucText-Eval. The main text, figures, tables and complete appendices support comparison, including matching language grammars and task examples. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, human performance, fine-tuning experiments and complexity analyses in Tables 1–2 and Figures 4–9.

after.justification: v3 reports original model and human evaluations, demonstration-count experiments, complexity analyses and comparisons of evaluation metrics in Tables 2–4 and Figures 4–7.

M1.justification: The abstract-tree, question-template and answer-discovery pipeline remains, as do the appendix grammars. However, Figure 2 replaces v1's node-count control with explicit depth, width and per-node field-count inputs. The PDFs do not establish whether this changes the generator's procedure or documents previously available controls.

E1.justification: The eight structured languages and 29 tasks remain, with matching appendix examples. v3 removes the ShareGPT-mixed general-text fine-tuning scenario evaluated in v1 Section 4.3 and extends the Hard evaluation to substantially longer structured inputs. These alter coverage within a largely retained task scope.

E2.justification: v1's main comparisons cover GPT-4, GPT4-Turbo, Minimax, Spark and Ernie-Turbo, alongside OpenLLaMA fine-tuning variants. v3 Tables 2–3 instead evaluate GPT-4o variants, Gemini 1.5, GLM-4, Qwen2, Llama 3.1 and Mistral models. PS-CoT and simple-three-shot comparisons are added, while the systematic fine-tuning comparisons disappear.

E3.justification: v1 describes 6,032 samples with a 9:2 training/testing partition; v3 specifies 3,712 Test and 2,088 Test-Hard samples with explicit depth/width strata. Primary scoring changes from GPT4-Turbo judging to ROUGE-L with scores below 0.75 set to zero. v3 also introduces a demonstration sweep through ten examples and a cross-metric evaluation subset, whose size is inconsistently stated as 300 outputs per model in Appendix B versus 1,000 samples per metric in Table 4.

E4.justification: v1's fine-tuning comparisons across languages and tasks and its training-loss plots are removed. v3 adds demonstration-count sensitivity, regular versus simple three-shot comparisons, and agreement between automated metrics and human judgments. The GPT4-Turbo length/node analysis becomes a multi-model depth/width analysis. Figure 7 also replaces the earlier case study's training stages with comparisons among newer models.

E5.justification: v3 Figure 5 adds standard-deviation summaries across models, languages and tasks at different complexity settings. These describe performance heterogeneity, not repeated-run uncertainty. The seed-42 settings remain unchanged between v1 Table 4 and v3 Table 9; no increase in runs or seeds is established.

E6.justification: The principal result matrices are replaced, additional metric-agreement results appear, and fine-tuning trajectories disappear. For example, v1 Table 2 reports GPT-4 Base at 65.0 and humans at 95.7 on Hard; v3 Table 3 reports GPT-4o-Turbo Base at 51.1, three-shot at 69.5, and humans at 92.6. Different models, datasets and scoring prevent interpreting these as matched performance changes. Some v3 prose conflicts with its tables, including retaining the 95.7 human figure in Section 5.2.

T1.justification: The formal language grammars and recursive task rules in v1 Appendix F reappear in v3 Appendix E with formatting changes. No substantive theorem, proof, mathematical derivation or formal assumption is added or removed.

C1.justification: v1 presents the benchmark as both an evaluation and model-improvement resource, prominently claiming that fine-tuning improves all structured languages but not every task. v3 removes those broad training contributions from the abstract, introduction and conclusion, concentrating on controlled-difficulty reasoning evaluation and model–human gaps. The central claim that existing LLMs struggle with complex structures remains.

C2.justification: v1 interprets generally harmful rule hints as evidence that models do not understand parsing rules; v3 emphasizes hints compensating for reasoning weaknesses. v3 adds explanations involving excessive demonstrations and overfitting, and argues for ROUGE-L's agreement with humans, replacing v1's emphasis on its potentially distorting format requirements. Fine-tuning interpretations are largely removed, although Section 5.6 retains a training-progress explanation inconsistent with the revised case-study figure.

D1.justification: v3 supplies more specific model checkpoint and API identifiers and explains depth, width and field-count controls. It removes v1's training hyperparameter block, including batch size, learning rate and training steps. Hardware, seed and generation-setting disclosures remain, as do the substantive appendix prompt templates and rule hints.

R1.justification: Related Work is substantially rewritten, shifting from code-structure models and tabular-learning studies toward tool graphs, graph foundation models and newer structured-data benchmarks. Added discussions include ControlLLM, TEMPTABQA, TableLLM and Struc-Bench, while several earlier code-analysis and tabular-baseline references disappear. This changes research positioning beyond citation-format updates.

P1.justification: The benchmark and title are renamed, the abstract and related work are extensively rewritten, and the analysis section is reorganized around new evaluation questions. The fine-tuning sections and checklist are removed, and appendix sections are rearranged. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column presentation. Benchmark statistics move into a redesigned main-text table; the decomposition and generation diagrams are revised; fine-tuning plots are replaced by demonstration and metric-analysis displays. Result tables and the case-study figure are restructured, while retained appendix examples are reduced and arranged together across columns.

improvement.justification: v3 gains broader model comparisons, explicit difficulty strata and human–metric agreement analysis, while losing systematic fine-tuning evidence. However, important reporting conflicts undermine the additions: Table 2 gives Qwen2-7B Base an overall score of 30.0 although every language score exceeds 54; Appendix B and Table 4 disagree on validation sample size; and Section 5.6 describes training stages absent from Figure 7. These problems affect the interpretation and reproducibility of central evidence, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
